title: DataTrail Portfolio Course
text:
Start Here
This course website is a reference for students in the Code in the Schools DataTrail course. As you complete the course’s portfolio assignments, it is our hope that this will be a useful step-by-step guide to showcasing your work. This course will expand on some of the best practices for online data science professional portfolios.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.1 Why create a portfolio
A portfolio has many benefits, here are just a few:  1. Helping with reflecting on your professional experiences and setting goals for the future  2. An easy visual resume with links to tangible work that’s quite difficult to find and understand on a static CV or resume. It shows evidence of you using the skills that many without portfolios may only have listed on a resume!  3. Shows your self-starter spirit, which boosts competitiveness for internships, jobs, and college.  4. Helps people find you, including future collaborators, colleagues, and mentors/mentees.
References: MIT Career Advising & Professional Development Office Intuit Blog

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.2 Setting up your starter site
Before we get started, first you’ll need a portfolio website to work from. We’ll be hosting our portfolios with GitHub Pages, which is a particularly common hosting tool for data scientists. Others include Adobe Portfolio, Google Sites, and Cargo for example.
You should be logged into your GitHub account with the username  if available. If not available, it should be the closest variant, like , , or . If you want to change your GitHub account name, instructions for how to do so can be found in the GitHub section of this course here.
The template portfolio website for DataTrail students can be found at the following GitHub repository: portfolio template. Once you’ve navigated to this repo,  1. Click Use this template  2. Then Create a new repository, and name it <username>.github.io using your exact GitHub username.
Here’s what your site will look like.
You’ll need to make two additional GitHub repositories for Homework 1, so let’s make those now. You’ll use the ‘Create Repository’ button:  2. Blog: name it blog.  3. Capstone:, you can name this repo your project name, but datatrail26-capstone is fine for now if you don’t have this in mind yet. 
The starter site was created using HTML, CSS, and JS. We’ll get more into what these languages are, resources for how you can customize your site beyond what’s outlined in the majority of this guide in Section 8. For now, let’s proceed to the portfolio prerequisites outlined in Section 2.

title: 3  Your home page
text:
3.1 Fill in index.html
Lots of simple commits to make on your index.html and optional ones on your styles.css.

title: 3  Your home page
text:
Where it says ‘DataTrail Student Name’, replace it with your name
Where it says ‘Data Science Student’, you can either keep this or replace this with another short tidbit about what you do/what your data science interests are
You’ll replace the social links here with your profile links you’ve created (Github, Linkedin, Kaggle).
Where it says name[at]school.edu, you’ll write your school email
Where it says name[at]codeintheschools.edu, you’ll write your Code in the Schools email address.
You’ll write your bio where the lorem ipsum boilerplate text is.
Relevant Coursework: List your classes you’ve enjoyed or done particularly well in. Feel free to list your GPA or grades in these classes.
Experience: If you have a job, school clubs, volunteer experiences, internships, programs you’ve participated in, or research assistantships you’ve done that you want to highlight – list them here!

title: 3  Your home page
text:
3.2 Images and documents

You’ll upload your headshot to the images/ folder
You’ll also upload your CV (as a PDF) to the documents/ folder
Important! If the names of these documents are different than the template names (Sample_CV CiTS.pdf and my_headshot.jpeg), you will go into the index.html and change these relative path names to point to the name of your CV and/or your headshot instead.

title: 3  Your home page
text:
3.3 Customize fonts and colors (optional)
Still in index.html, there are some design updates you can make. Namely, to fonts and icons:
Right now the font in here is ‘Manrope’. You can browse new fonts at this link: - Google Fonts To change this font, you’ll click ‘Get Font’ once you click on the font that you want. You can get the embed code for either ‘One value’ the one that is currently selected or the ‘Full axis’ (all of the weight options). I used and recommend two font weights, one bold and one not bold, but feel free to take creative liberty. Where it says ’Embed code in the

of your html’, you’ll copy this code and replace the equivalent lines for the template fonts. If you have questions about this, feel free to ask your professor. You will also want to change this where the ‘font-family’ is defined for the .body section in the styles.css file And where ‘font-weight’ is defined for the h2 under your headshot, you will change it to one of the font weights that you downloaded.
You may notice there are icons next to your CV, and for your socials links. If you want to change these, add more, or just check out the other options, you can do so here: - Font Awesome icons Wherever you see: i class=… in your index.html, this is an icon. You can update these or add them where appropriate (perhaps in your projects.html links when we get there).
In styles.css, the color scheme for most of the site elements is set. The teal accent color in the template can be changed by changing the hex code listed next to –link-color. Here is a site to browse for new colors. You can also do this in several code editors, like VSCode. Feel free to ask your instructor for a quick tutorial on this: - HTML color picker

title: 4  Populating your links
5  news.html
text:
Take a moment to think through recent academic and professional accomplishments You were accepted into DataTrail! Other things that count as news: 1. classes 2. grades and test scores 3. awards 4. events, conferences, and competitions you’ve attended or participated in 5. new blog posts
Write a list of these in your notes and pick your favorites. Note the date they happened and update the news.html file

title: 6  projects.html
text:
A project is an item that has a deliverable that you would like to showcase (i.e. a paper, code, a repository, a presentation, a model, a video, data visualizations).
Right now the template project section has a card for:

A class project - a project from class (it can be DataTrail or from school),
Your blog, and
Your DataTrail capstone project:

Write in your notes the name or title for at least one project that could be classified as each of these Draft a short description And compile any links to your project’s deliverables. If you don’t want to link to an external Drive or DropBox for example, you’ll want to download these and upload them to the docs folder in your portfolio’s repository. There can be some benefits to using these online storage platforms, as for many of them you can readily see traffic link clicks are getting.
Right now, there are boilerplate photos in this section. In a later assignment, you’ll use your favorite plot as the capstone project photo.
Other links will be styled here later in the course: your slide deck link, and DataTrail Python notebook results (Chapter 8). If your capstone leads to a publication or presentation, you can link to that here too.
